parts:
Dear Len,

Thanks for your reply. I am sorry if I didn't make myself very
clear in the first message - here's a bit more background to the
problem.

I have been surveying hornbills in tropical rainforest using the
point count method. I recorded data by both visual and auditory
cues, however, I am analysing these data seperately as they
do give different detection functions.

My problem with "negative" cluster size bias is indeed different from
the one described in the Distance sampling book where clusters away
from the trackline or point tend to be more visible if they are
large. I presume this problem is more prominent in open areas (e.g.
at sea), where one can see to relatively far distances. As hornbills
are large, noisy birds and a single bird can be readily detected
calling 250m away, my problem is not so much one of missing
observations of small clusters but of underestimating the number of
individuals in a cluster at larger distances. In dense forest,
although it is easy to count the number of individuals in a tree 10m
away, one is likely to underestimate (by both visual and auditory
cues) the number in a group 80m away that are obsured by foliage.

I had therefore proposed to generate a mean cluster size from visual
contacts at shorter distances and then use this value when working
out density estimates based on the 'auditory cue' detection function
(NB. not pooling visual and auditory cue data for the
detection function).

Thanks for your other tips, I would also appreciate hearing
from anyone else who has experienced similar problems with their
methodology or has used a similar method of analysis.

Regards,

Alexis Cahill

P.S. Apologies for sending two copies of my last message but when
e-mailing to the distance address I always receive an error message
claiming my attempt was unsucessful. I have noted that at least one
other mailer has this same problem.




Hi Alexis,

For some reason we on the list got two copies of your message. Perhaps you
pressed the "Send" button twice by accident?

Anyway, here are some initial thoughts. Perhaps others on the list have
better ideas, or can correct any mistakes I've made in the following...

> >My data was collected with contacts recorded as clusters. Distance
> >allows for detection of contacts decreasing away from 0m, but what
> >about detection of individuals within each cluster? Unsurprisingly,
> >this also decreases towards larger distances for my data.

Distance assumes that you measure the size of each cluster accurately. If
you have a tendency to underestimate the size of clusters far away, this will
need to be accounted for.

> >When I run the Distance program I receive a cluster size bias warning
> >i.e. groups closer to 0m are larger.

"Cluster size bias" in Distance terminology usually refers to the process
where in some studies clusters that are further away from the trackline or
point are more visible. For example, when surveying dolphins, large pods are
relatively easy to see at large distances because there tends to be lots of
dolphins surfacing at once, but small pods can easily be missed at large
distances. So, if you look at the data you find that there are both large
and small pods at small distances, but only large pods at large distances.
See the Distance sampling book (Buckland et al 1993), section 3.6 for more on
this.

One way to control for size bias is to do a regression of distance (or
estimated probability of detection, or the log of either of these) against
cluster size, and use the estimated cluster size at 0 distance (or prob of
detection of 1) as an estimate of the true mean cluster size. This type of
size bias correction is done by default in Distance (see the Model
Definition's Cluster Size tab).

You get a warning because your data goes the *opposite* way to the usual
situation: you have more larger clusters at close distances. In most studies
this would indicate a problem, which is why Distance generates a warning.

> >(However, when I run a
> >regression in SPSS I do not get a significant result. Is this because
> >the sigificance level is set differently for Distance?).

The default in Distance is to do the size bias regression regardless of the
statistical significance of the slope. This is because using the "adjusted"
cluster size will not bias the overall estimate and does not often decrease
the precision of the final estimate, even when there is no size bias in
reality; also because we don't particularly like significance tests as a
means of judging the biological importance of an effect (selection of the
alpha level is too arbitary for our liking). You can ask Distance to do the
adjustment only when the regression is significant, and can set the
significance level - see the Cluster Size tab.

> >If I truncate my data this gets rid of the problem, however, as some
> >of my sample sizes are small I don t want to loose too many contacts.
> >Is it o.k. to use the cluster size obtained from Visual only contacts
> >to give an average value that can be multiplied by the density of
> >contacts, D(s) obtained from Call contacts?

A general point:
>From this and the following paragraph, I gather that you are working on point
counts of bird species, and that you have recorded birds by both visual and
auditory cues. This can be problematic for distance sampling analysis, as
the detection curves for the two methods will likely differ dramatically and
the data often violate the "shape criterion". See the Distance book, figure
2.1 for an example of what can happen. See associated text for definition of
"shape criterion". So, you should do some cautious exploratory data analysis
before going ahead and pooling visual and auditory detections -- try fitting
a simple detection function to these two sets of data separately and looking
at the histograms to check you aren't going to get something nasty. You may
find that you can't pool the data, in which case you'll need to use post-
stratification to fit separate detection functions to each one (same as
fitting a separate detection function in different geographic strata, etc).

Now, back to clusters:
The size-bias remedies discussed in the Distance book, section 3.6, could
work for you. Firstly, truncation. You can use the Data Filter in Distance
to set a different truncation distance for cluster size estimation as for
detection function fitting. This way you can truncate the data to the
distance below which you're pretty sure you got accurate cluster size
measurements without affecting the detection function estimation. In this
case you'd set the model definition | cluster size option to use the average
of the cluster sizes (after truncation). Next regression. This may work (as
described above - just ignore the warning) -- however I would be hesitant to
use the fitted detection function (g(x)) as the independent variable --
instead I'd use distance (logged).

More sophisticated approaches are possible. For example, if you think the
visual observations were accurate cluster sizes, but not the auditory then,
as you suggest, you could use the visual observations to get the cluster
sizes. However, in this case I'd be even more concerned about pooling the
data to make a combined detection function...

> >On the same line, what about bird species where cluster size is
> >dependent on the time of year. When trying to obtain monthly
> >estimates of density is it o.k. to use Call contacts to obtain the
> >detection function for the year, but then base the cluster size on a
> >monthly average calculated using the Visual only data.

Don't know about using call contacts (I already talked about the need to look
at the data before pooling call and sightings contacts). Also have talked
already about other ways of getting at the cluster size problem. As for
pooling cluster size at one level and detection function at another, this is
probably fine. Usually, one would first try the detection functions by month
(using stratification) and then try them pooled over the year, and use some
measure such as AIC to tell which gave the better fit. However, you may well
not have enough data to do the monthly detection functions with any
robustness.

> >This seems to be the obvious way of overcoming these problems but I
> >would appreciate someone validating the method for me. Does Distance
> >have options to do this automatically or is it a matter of working out
> >D(s) and manually multiplying this up by cluster size?

If you use the "visual only" approach, then you'd have to work out density of
birds from D(s) and estimated s by hand.

Hope this helps,

- Len


--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator
Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland
